# REPORT — 12 wire items, one newsroom question

*Generated by `report.py` from `ledger.json`. Every number below is a ledger read; nothing is carried over from the run's own logs. The strategy this executes was pre-registered in `STRATEGY.md` before the first call — see the hashes in `runlog.json`.*

Pre-registration hashes, taken before the first call: `STRATEGY.md` `88f9462f6f95`, `corpus.py` `fc8a300642c9`, `strategy.py` `41dbf5a3f126`, `run.py` `647640640c1c`

*`STRATEGY.md`, `corpus.py` and `strategy.py` — the three that constitute the pre-registration — are unchanged since. `run.py` is not: it was edited mid-run to catch transport errors and to stop retrying a hung call three times, after the first attempt died of exactly that. The stamp above is the pre-edit hash, and the discrepancy is disclosed rather than re-stamped. No axis, threshold, weighting or rule was touched.*

Ledger: **701 opinions**.

## 0. Read this first

The corpus is **synthetic** and was written for this experiment by the same kind of process that reads it. Nothing here is a finding about the news. Everything here is a finding about **the instrument**, which is a legitimate object of measurement (Pillar I: instruments are things) and the only one this corpus can support.

Grading, applied to every conclusion at the end: **calibrated** (laws held, paths agreed, concordance with frozen ground), **coherent** (laws held, paths agreed, no ground), **claim** (single path, no law, no ground).

### What this run found

* **One call bought the sharpest negative result.** The listwise ordering path returned a valid permutation that reproduced the order it was shown (ρ = 0.979 against presentation order). It passed its law and measured nothing. §7.
* **The instrument reads an axis differently depending on what it read first.** On `follow_up`, every base/twin disagreement went the same way (+1.00 mean shift, 4 of 4 items). A context effect, not variance: repetition will not average it away. §2.
* **A grounding validator pulled the instrument toward wrong answers.** On the three items whose true count is not printed in them, `TokenSubset` refused one and let two through at numbers that were printed in the text but were not the answer (14 for 16, 340 for 385). Confident, validated, wrong. §6.
* **The stated `p` is a real signal on one axis and a formality on another.** It separated hits from misses on `people_affected` and not on `horizon`. Calibration is per axis; a pooled figure would have hidden both. §5.
* **A validator can be the thing that is wrong.** `isoCountry` scored four correct readings at zero, because the vendored table holds 35 countries. Concordance on that axis was 12/12. §6.
* **The zero-call pass earned its keep.** A wrong dateline weekday, a duplicate pair, and the coverage limits of the reference table — all before a single call, and all by mechanisms genuinely unlike the model's. §1.

## 1. The pre-pass, which spent nothing

Zero calls. 12 items, 850 words, 69 numbers.

| signal | mechanism | fired on |
|---|---|---|
| `shingle5` | 5-word order | — (nothing) |
| `unigram` | vocabulary | `n11/n12` |
| `fingerprint` | dateline date + number multiset | `n11/n12` |

The one duplicate pair is `n11`/`n12`. Note **which signal missed it**: 5-shingle Jaccard scored it 0.0196, far under the pre-registered 0.5, even though it ranked the pair first. Unigram Jaccard scored 0.6 and the number fingerprint matched exactly. Three signals were declared together precisely so that this could be observed instead of tuned away: a paraphrased duplicate defeats word-order shingling, and only a mechanism that ignores word order catches it.

Dateline faults found without a call: `n05` — contradicted by the proleptic Gregorian calendar: 2026-08-03 is a Monday, not Wednesday.

The vendored ISO 3166-1 table covers 35 countries, so 4 datelines (n02, n08, n11, n12) sit outside it. That is a property of the *validator*, not of the items — a reference instrument with partial exposure, measured before it was trusted.

## 2. Reliability, which caps everything below it

Four items (`n01`, `n06`, `n09`, `n10`) read twice: once in the declared axis order, once on a twin entity with the order reversed, so every reading saw a different set of resolved siblings in its snapshot.

| axis | scale | n | exact | within one step | unresolved both passes | kept? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `country` | nominal | 4 | 100% | 100% | — | yes |
| `people_affected` | ratio | 2 | 100% | 100% | `n10` (one pass only: `n06`) | yes |
| `certainty` | ordinal | 4 | 100% | 100% | — | yes |
| `horizon` | ordinal | 4 | 100% | 100% | — | yes |
| `ratio_claim` | nominal | 3 | 100% | 100% | — (one pass only: `n10`) | yes |
| `severity` | ordinal | 4 | 50% | 100% | — | yes |
| `follow_up` | ordinal | 4 | 0% | 100% | — | **dropped** |

Cells that failed to resolve in **both** passes are excluded from the rates and listed instead: reproducibly unreadable is a real property of the instrument, but it is not agreement about a value, and folding it in either way would be a lie about the same number.

Pre-registered rule: an axis below 50% exact agreement is dropped from the weighted aggregation. Dropped: `follow_up`.

Four items is a thin base and these rates carry wide intervals. They are a **ceiling**, not an estimate: no claim further down may be more confident than the axis it rests on was reproducible.

### The disagreement has a direction

On the twin pass the axes are read in reverse, so an axis read *first* there was read *last* on the base pass, after its siblings had already resolved into the snapshot. Signed difference, twin minus base:

| axis | n | disagreed | mean shift | up | down | every disagreement one way |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `certainty` | 4 | 0 | +0.00 | 0 | 0 | — (no disagreement) |
| `horizon` | 4 | 0 | +0.00 | 0 | 0 | — (no disagreement) |
| `severity` | 4 | 2 | +0.50 | 2 | 0 | **yes** |
| `follow_up` | 4 | 4 | +1.00 | 4 | 0 | **yes** |

For `severity`, `follow_up` every single disagreement points the same way. That is not variance — it is a **context effect**, and the distinction matters more than the size: variance shrinks when you average repeated readings, and a context effect does not. Reading an axis cold and reading it after its siblings are two different measurements of two different things, and the ledger says so in the only way that counts, by disagreeing consistently.

The instrument read 2. Counting that as an instrument error overstates the error — the ambiguity is in **the measurand**, which the corpus author wrote and the instrument did not. ## 5. Is the instrument's own `p` a probability?

Every reading on a grounded axis, bucketed by the probability the instrument stated for it, against how often it was right.

| stated p | n | hits | observed (95% Wilson) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 1 | 0 | 0.00 [0.00, 0.79] |
| 0.4 | 1 | 0 | 0.00 [0.00, 0.79] |
| 0.9 | 1 | 0 | 0.00 [0.00, 0.79] |
| 1.0 | 45 | 44 | 0.98 [0.88, 1.00] |

Bucketed rates on this few readings say little. The sharper question is whether a low `p` lands on the readings that turned out wrong — separation, per axis:

| axis | hits | misses | mean p on hits | mean p on misses | separation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `country` | 12 | 0 | 1 | — | — |
| `people_affected` | 10 | 2 | 1 | 0.25 | +0.75 |
| `certainty` | 12 | 0 | 0.97 | — | — |
| `horizon` | 10 | 2 | 0.98 | 0.93 | +0.06 |

On `people_affected` the stated `p` is **doing work**: the readings that turned out wrong are the ones the instrument was least sure of. That is the single most useful thing an instrument can do that a plain extractor cannot.

On `horizon` it is **not**: the wrong readings came with the same confidence as the right ones. A `p` that does not separate is a formality, and on this axis it should not be propagated into anything downstream.

* `n02` / `country` / `isoCountry` (p=0.0): unknown in iso-3166-1:2020: KE
* `n08` / `country` / `isoCountry` (p=0.0): unknown in iso-3166-1:2020: NG
* `n11` / `country` / `isoCountry` (p=0.0): unknown in iso-3166-1:2020: PH
* `n12` / `country` / `isoCountry` (p=0.0): unknown in iso-3166-1:2020: PH
* `n10` / `people_affected` / `tokenSubset[text,kinds=[numbers]]` (p=0.0): absent from text: 0.0
* `n07` / `ratio_claim` / `calculator` (p=0.0): 4200 / 11 = 381.8181818181818, not 420.0
* `n05` / `ratio_claim` / `schema[{expression:str,result:float}]` (p=0.0): value: expected an object, got NoneType

**Read the `country` row backwards.** `isoCountry` scored 4 of 12 readings at zero, yet concordance with the frozen ground on that axis is 12/12. Every one of those 'violations' is a correct reading of a country the vendored 35-entry table does not contain. The validator was right to be attached non-necessary: as a veto it would have destroyed four correct answers. **A law reading is a reading about the pair (candidate, validator), and when they disagree the record does not say which one is wrong** — here the frozen ground does, and it says the validator was.

**Cells that never resolved.** Every candidate was scored below the veto line by a `necessary` belief until the budget ran out. Per axis: `ratio_claim` — `n05`; `people_affected` — `n10`.

The two have nothing in common but their outcome. `n10.people_affected` is a real judgement: `TokenSubset` looked at the candidate and refused it. `n05.ratio_claim` is not a judgement at all — three completions in a row carried no `value` key, so `Schema` was handed `None` and said so. **A dead cell and a refused cell look identical from the outside and mean opposite things**, and only the reason strings in the ledger separate them.

### The predicted tension, and the shape it actually took

`STRATEGY.md` §4 predicted, before any call, that `TokenSubset` attached `necessary` to `people_affected` would collide with a measurand that asks for sums: `n03` (2 dead + 14 injured = 16) and `n06` (340 pupils + 45 staff = 385) both have a correct answer that appears nowhere in their text. The collision happened. It did not take the shape predicted.

| item | truth | what the instrument settled on | in the text? | vetoed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `n03` | `16` | `14` | **yes** | no |
| `n06` | `385` | `340` | **yes** | no |
| `n10` | `0` | *never resolved* | no | yes |

Only one of the three ended in a refusal. On the other two the instrument, pushed by the veto, **abandoned the arithmetic and returned a number that was printed in the item** — 14 (the injured, dropping the dead) and 340 (the pupils, dropping the staff). Those readings passed every validator and were wrong.

That is worse than the failure that was predicted, and more useful. A grounding validator does not merely block derived quantities; it **exerts a pull toward whatever is printed**, and the instrument follows it. Anti-hallucination and arithmetic are in direct conflict, and one has to give: either the validator learns about sums, or the measurand stops asking for them, or the axis is split into a stated-figure axis and a derived-figure axis. The experiment cannot pick. It can show the choice is forced, and that leaving it unmade produces confident wrong answers rather than visible failures.

The one genuine refusal was `n10`, and it was **not** predicted: its true count is 0, because no people were affected, and the digit 0 appears nowhere in an item about reefs. The zero case is the same collision in a shape the pre-registration missed.

## 7. Three orders on one question

| pair of paths | Spearman ρ | n | what it is worth |
|---|---|---|---|
| pro absolute vs pro listwise | 0.279 | 12 | **void** — the listwise path reproduced the input order (see below), so this correlates with presentation order, not with follow-up value |
| flash absolute vs pro absolute | 0.45 | 12 | different model *and* different context (warm vs cold) — confounded, reported for completeness only |
| flash absolute vs pro listwise | 0.235 | 12 | **void** — the listwise path reproduced the input order (see below), so this correlates with presentation order, not with follow-up value |

Two of the three rows are struck out by the check that follows them. What survives is one confounded comparison at ρ = 0.45, which is not enough to order twelve items and is not claimed to be.

**n_eff, stated plainly.** `flash` and `pro` are the same model family on the same server reading the same bytes. Mechanism overlap is high, exposure overlap is total. Two such readings are worth barely more than one: no conclusion in this report is justified by "two models agreed".

Listwise permutation (best first): `n01 > n03 > n04 > n02 > n05 > n06 > n07 > n08 > n09 > n10 > n11 > n12`  
The permutation law held: no drops, no inventions, no repeats.

**Discrimination check for an ordering.** Correlation of the returned order against the order the items were *presented* in: ρ = 0.979 over n = 12. 3 of 12 items moved at all: `n03`, `n04`, `n02`.

This is the result that governs the whole section. A valid permutation that reproduces the input order **passes the permutation law while measuring nothing** — the law was never in danger, so satisfying it earned no confidence at all (Pillar III: coherence you built in earns nothing; a constant-output instrument passes every law and is worthless). Any agreement between this path and another is therefore agreement with the input ordering, not evidence about follow-up value, and **the listwise path is withdrawn from the deliverable.** The one call it cost was the cheapest finding in the run.

Axes carried into the aggregation: `severity`, `people_affected`, `certainty`, `horizon`. Dropped for unreliability: none.

An honest footnote on that rule. The axis it actually failed is `follow_up`, which was never an *input* to the aggregation — it is the instrument's own answer to the stakeholder question, shown separately below. So the pre-registered floor bit exactly nothing in the aggregation, and it is reported here rather than quietly counted as a rule that passed.

**Items excluded from the ranking entirely:** `n10` — at least one axis there ended vetoed, and a vetoed candidate is not a reading. They are ranked nowhere rather than ranked low: an item the instrument could not read is not thereby unimportant.

Ranks are aggregated, **never raw ordinal values** — a weighted sum of ordinal scores is not a licensed statistic. Weights are human-owned and printed in full; because `STRATEGY.md` declared magnitudes but not the *direction* of `certainty` (chase the confirmed story, or the unconfirmed one?), every weighting is run both ways rather than resolved after the fact.

* **harm-first (certainty +)** — `n12` > `n11` > `n05` > `n03` > `n02` > `n09` …
* **harm-first (certainty -)** — `n12` > `n11` > `n05` > `n03` > `n02` > `n07` …
* **verifiability-first (certainty +)** — `n03` > `n05` > `n12` > `n11` > `n09` > `n01` …
* **verifiability-first (certainty -)** — `n06` > `n07` > `n05` > `n08` > `n12` > `n11` …
* **scale-first (certainty +)** — `n12` > `n11` > `n09` > `n05` > `n02` > `n03` …
* **scale-first (certainty -)** — `n12` > `n11` > `n09` > `n05` > `n02` > `n07` …

**Robust:** in the top four under *every* weighting and both directions: `n05`.

**Weight-sensitive:** top four under some weightings and not others: `n03`, `n06`, `n07`, `n08`, `n09`, `n11`, `n12`. These are the items where the answer is a *value judgement the newsroom owns*, not a measurement.

The instrument's own `follow_up` axis, for comparison and never fused into the above: `n03` > `n11` > `n01` > `n02` > `n04` > `n05` > `n07` > `n08` > `n12` > `n06` > `n09` > `n10`

## 10. What is absent

* **The corpus.** Synthetic, 12 items, shared authorship with the reader. Every rate here is an upper bound on real copy, not an estimate of it.
* **Independent mechanism.** Two models of one family behind one endpoint. The only genuinely dissimilar paths in this experiment are the classical ones — shingling, the number fingerprint, `CalendarFact`, `Calculator`, `TokenSubset` — and they are the ones that produced the crispest results.
* **Independent exposure.** Every path read the same bytes. Nothing here can detect a defect that was in the corpus before measurement began.
* **Axes nobody measured.** Cost to the newsroom of chasing a story, audience interest, source reliability, competitive exclusivity, legal exposure. A follow-up decision made on this matrix alone is made on a quarter of the relevant axes.
* **The absent population.** Every wire nobody filed, every story killed before it reached a desk. No internal path sees it.
* **Causal questions.** None asked, none answerable: dissimilar paths reading one non-randomised corpus share its confounding exactly.

## 11. Grading

| conclusion | grade | why |
|---|---|---|
| The `n11`/`n12` duplicate pair | **calibrated** | two classical signals of different mechanism agreed; verifiable by inspection with no model in the loop |
| `n05`'s dateline weekday is wrong | **calibrated** | pure computation against the proleptic Gregorian calendar |
| Arithmetic fault found in n07 (1 of 2 planted) | **calibrated** | adjudicated by `calculate`, not by the instrument, which only transcribed the claim |
| `n05`'s planted fault (30% stated where 60000/250000 = 24%) was **missed** | **n/a** | not a judgement error — the cell never resolved, so `Calculator` was never handed a claim to check. A law cannot fire on a reading that does not exist, and an unresolved cell is therefore a silent gap in coverage rather than a clean negative |
| `country` read at 100% concordance | **calibrated** | measured against a frozen human assignment; interval [0.76, 1.00] on n=12 |
| `people_affected` read at 83% concordance | **calibrated** | measured against a frozen human assignment; interval [0.55, 0.95] on n=12 |
| `certainty` read at 100% concordance | **calibrated** | measured against a frozen human assignment; interval [0.76, 1.00] on n=12 |
| `horizon` read at 83% concordance | **calibrated** | measured against a frozen human assignment; interval [0.55, 0.95] on n=12 |
| Any ordering of the twelve items | **claim** | no ground exists for `follow_up`; the paths that agree share mechanism and exposure, so their agreement is cheap |
| `severity` readings | **claim** | no ground, one model family, and the axis is a judgement the corpus cannot settle |

## 12. What it cost

Recomputed from the ledger, not from the runner's own counters: a reading on a twin entity or a pair entity bought validation, everything else bought findings. One model opinion is one round is one call, except that a completion the transport had to re-ask for leaves no opinion — so these are a floor.

| tier | rounds in the ledger |
|---|---|
| findings | 110 |
| validation | 51 |
| **total** | **161** |

32% of the spend bought no findings at all. That is the price of the confidence in §2, §6 and §8, and it is stated separately so the buyer can see what confidence costs.

Transport counters, **for the resumed segment only**: 71 flash calls (59,658 prompt / 44,744 completion tokens), 14 pro calls (11,263 / 10,501), 55 minutes of wall clock on a server that serves one request at a time.

These 85 counted calls are **not** the whole run and the gap to the 161 rounds above is mostly not the re-ask ladder. The first attempt died partway through phase 3 — three consecutive 300-second read timeouts on `n03.people_affected`, one of the veto-loop cells, raising `EngineError`. Its calls are in the ledger and not in these counters, because the counters live in the process and the ledger lives on disk. That is the argument for persistence made the hard way: the run resumed from the record and lost nothing but its own bookkeeping.
